text: Assessing the viability of sufolane-based electrolytes in lithium-sulfur batteries: Challenges and limitations Dong Zheng , Dantong Qiu , Yang Qin , Xiaoxiao Zhang , Miao Liu , Huainan Qu , Tianyao Ding , Deyang Qu * Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Engineering and Applied Science, University of Wisconsin Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI, 53211, USA H I G H L I G H T S • Emerging sulfolane-based electrolyte is investigated. • High viscosity of sulfolane electrolytes was found suppressing polysulfide shuttle. • LiNO3 is essential to reduce the shuttle effect at higher temperatures in sulfolane.

A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Li-S battery HPLC Polysulfide shuttle Sulfolane electrolyte LiNO3 additive A B S T R A C T The polysulfide shuttle is a well-known side reaction in rechargeable Lithium-Sulfur batteries with nonaqueous liquid electrolytes.
To address this thermodynamically favorable reaction, extensive research has focused on developing novel electrolyte systems.
Recently, sulfolane-based electrolyte has gained attention due to their potential to inhibit the polysulfide shuttle in Li-S batteries.
In this preliminary investigation, we analyzed the reactivity of polysulfides with Li anode using HPLC and studied the viscosity of various electrolytes at different temperatures.
Our findings suggested that high viscosity of the sulfolane electrolyte could contribute to its ability to suppress the polysulfide shuttle.
Additionally, we demonstrated that the presence of a LiNO3 additive is crucial for mitigating the polysulfide shuttle effect in sulfolane electrolytes, especially at elevated temperature. 1.
Introduction Nonaqueous liquid electrolytes are essential in lithium-based rechargeable batteries, as they maintain the mass transfer and the ionic conductivity.
Those electrolytes must exhibit both chemical and electrochemical stability during redox reactions occurring at the bat­ tery’s cathodes and anodes [1–6].
For state-of-the-art lithium-ion bat­ teries (LiBs), the most commonly used electrolyte is lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6) in a carbonate mixture with organic or inorganic additives.
However, carbonate-based electrolytes are chemi­ cally incompatible with lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries, particularly when using elemental sulfur (S8) as the cathode active materials [7].
Current research has focused on using lithium bis(tri­ fluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSi) in a dimethoxyethane (DME) and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) mixture with lithium nitrate (LiNO3) as additive [3, 7].

This ether-based electrolyte has demonstrated moderate polysulfide solubility, good chemical and electrochemical stability, and high sulfur utilization, along with improved redox reversibility for Li-S batteries.
As a result, Li-S batteries using this ether-based electrolyte demonstrate enhanced cycling stability and a significant reduction in the notorious “polysulfide shuttle effect”.
However, the cycling stability of Li-S batteries with this ether-based electrolyte still falls short of that observed in Li-ion batteries using carbonate-based electrolyte.
Additionally, the continuous decomposi­ tion of the LiNO3 additive on the lithium anode raises concerns about the long-term stability of Li-S batteries [3].

Consequently, the search for novel electrolytes that can improve long-term cycling stability and minimize (or even eliminate) the “pol­ ysulfide shuttle effect” remains central focus of Li-S battery research.

Various alternative electrolytes have been explored, including those based on ionic liquids [8], poly-glymes [9], Ɛ-caprolactam/acetamide [10], fluorinated ethers [11,12], 1,3-dimethyl-2-imidazolidinone (DMI) [13], fluorinated pyridine [14].

While SL has a similar donor number to DME and DOL solvents [39], it boasts a high dielectric constant (leading to high polysulfide solubility), a high flash point, and superior oxidative stability making it a promising solvent for the elec­ trolytes of Li-S batteries.
Remarkably, the SL-based electrolytes, even without LiNO3 as shuttling inhibitor, have shown minimal “polysulfide shuttle effect” in Li-S batteries cycling at room temperature.
In this work, we explored the electrochemical performance of Li-S batteries and the chemical stability of Li metal with polysulfides at elevated temperature when using SL-based electrolytes.
We also dis­ cussed the possible reasons behind the minimal shuttle effect observed with these electrolytes. 2.
Experimental section 2.1.

Chemicals Sulfur (99.98 %), lithium sulfide (Li2S, 99.98 %), lithium nitrate (LiNO3,99.99 %), HPLC grade methanol, HPLC grade water, methyl triflate, sulfolane (SL) (from Sigma), dimethoxyethane (DME), 1,3-diox­ olane (DOL), and lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSi) (battery grade from 3M) were purchased and used without further treatment. 2.2.

Sample preparation and methods The polysulfide solutions used in this work were 0.1 M stoichio­ metric Li2S6 in various electrolytes including 1.5 M LiTFSi/DME/DOL (1:1), 1.0 M LiTFSi/DME/DOL(1:1) with 0.5 M LiNO3, 1.5 M LiTFSi/SL, 1.0 M LiTFSi/SL with 0.5 M LiNO3.

These solutions were prepared by mixing S8 and Li2S (molar ratio of 5:8, to form stoichiometric Li2S6) in the different electrolytes, followed by stirring for 48 h at room tem­ perature in Ar-filled glovebox (Innovative Technology).

The chemical stability of Li metal against 0.1 M Li2S6 in the different electrolytes were tested by adding 50 mg lithium chip into sample vials with air-tight caps, containing 1.0 mL of the polysulfide solution in each electrolyte.
After vertexing the polysulfide solutions with the lithium chips for 5 min, the vials were stored at room temperature or at 60 ◦C for 4 days.
Finally, specific amount of the polysulfide solutions was deriv­ atized with methyl triflate in air-tight HPLC sample vials before removed from the glovebox for HPLC analysis.
The derivatization of the polysulfide solution was carried out as following: 950 μL of DME and 50 μL of methyl triflate were added into a 2 mL air-tight HPLC sample vial.
The mixture was vortexed for 1 min.
Then 50 μL of the polysulfide solution was added and the mixture was vortexed for an additional 2 min.
This process converted the polysulfides (Sn 2−) into organosulfides (CH3SnCH3) which were stable under HPLC mobile phase conditions and can be separated based on the chain length of sulfur [40–42].

A Shimadzu LC-20AD quaternary pump. equipped with a Shimadzu SIL-20A autosampler was used to deliver a methanol/water mobile phase through a Shimadzu C18 column (4.6*50 mm) at a flow rate of 0.70 mL/min.
The injection volume for the derivatized samples was 5 μL.

A binary gradient of mobile phases was used to elute the injected sample under the following condition: 25 % methanol (75 % water) at 0 min, 100 % methanol at 10 min, maintained until 23 min and back to 25 % methanol at 26 min.
The entire flow from the HPLC was introduced into the Shimadzu SPD-M20A detector, and the full wavelength range from 190 to 800 nm was recorded by Shimadzu LabSolutions Lite soft­ ware.
The chromatograms discussed in this work were replotted from collected data at 230 nm.
Sulfur cathodes were prepared by first mixing S (60%wt) with CMK3 mesoporous carbon (20%wt) through grinding.
The mixture was then sealed in an autoclave filled with argon and heated at 170 ◦C for 12 h.
After cooling down to room temperature, carbon black Super C-65(10% wt) and PVDF binder (10%wt) were added into the mixture, with N- Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) as solvent to form homogenous slurry.
This slurry was coated onto an alumina foil by a doctor-blade coater, and vacuum-dried at 60 ◦C for 12 h.
Finally, the electrode sheet was punched into disks and transferred into an argon-filled glovebox (both oxygen and moisture are less than 5 ppm) for 24 h before being tested.
The sulfur cathodes have a theoretical areal sulfur loading around 1.5 mg cm−2.
All battery tests were conducted in two-electrode CR2032 coin cells at either room temperature or at 60 ◦C.
Each battery used 15 μL of different electrolytes, with a Celgard 3401 membrane as the separator and lithium chip as the anodes.
After assembled in the Ar-filled glove­ box, all batteries were rested for 12 h before electrochemical testing.
For cycling tests, a galvanostatic discharge/charge procedure was conduct­ ed between 1.7 and 2.9 V at a constant rate of 0.05 C for all batteries by a battery testing system (Arbin BT2000).
For the elevated temperature test, the batteries were cycled at 60 ◦C in a temperature and humidity chamber (CSZ Z8 Plus).
The viscosity measurements of different electrolytes and solvents were performed using a viscometer (Brookfield DV-II+ Pro) with a water bath to control the temperature. 3.

Results and discussion As shown in Fig. 1(A), at room temperature, Li-S battery (based on the same S8/CMK3 composite cathodes) using 1.5 M LiTFSi/DME/DOL electrolyte exhibits a noticeable “polysulfide shuttle effect” due to the lack of LiNO3.
In contrast, as shown in Fig. 1(B), the Li-S battery with 1.5 M LiTFSi/SL electrolyte shows no significant “polysulfide shuttle effect” even after 200 cycles, despite not having the LiNO3 additive.
Further analysis of the chemical reactivity of lithium metal with 0.1 M Li2S6 solutions in either sulfolane electrolyte or in DME/DOL elec­ trolyte was conducted using HPLC.
The results illustrated in Fig. 2 indicated that the polysulfide solution in the sulfolane electrolyte is less reactive with lithium metal compared to the polysulfide solution in DME/DOL electrolyte.

This is clearly shown in Fig. 2(B), where the polysulfide profile of the DME/DOL electrolyte after 4 days of contact with lithium metal differs significantly from the original polysulfide solution, as shown in Fig. 2 (A).
The chromatographic peaks corre­ sponding to S3 2−and S4 2−increased while those belonging to S6 2−, S7 2−, S8 2− and S8 decreased after the reaction [41].

On the other hand, the polysulfide profile in Fig. 2 (F) (representing sulfolane electrolyte after 4 days of contact with lithium metal) is quite similar to the original sulfolane electrolyte shown in Fig. 2 (E), with only a noticeable change of the chromatographic peak corresponding to S8.

Both electrochemical cycling data (Fig. 1) and HPLC analysis (Fig. 2) indicate that the “polysulfide shuttle effect” in Li/S battery with sulfo­ lane electrolyte is minimized, if not eliminated, even without LiNO3 additive.

Unfortunately, at elevated temperatures (60 ◦C), both Li-S batteries using sulfolane electrolyte and DME/DOL electrolyte without LiNO3 additive exhibit the polysulfide shuttle effect, though to different ex­ tents, as shown in Fig. 1 (C) and 1 (D).
In the case of the Li-S battery with DME/DOL electrolyte (without LiNO3), the shuttle effect is pronounced, preventing the battery from cycling from the start as shown in Fig. 1 (C).

For the Li-S battery with sulfolane electrolyte (without LiNO3), the shuttle effect becomes noticeable after 5 discharge/charge cycles (with about 10 % overcharging), and the battery fails to cycle after 35 discharge/charge cycles due to the severe and notorious shuttle effect as shown in Fig. 1 (D).
The HPLC analysis in Fig. 2, which examines the chemical stability of Li metal with polysulfide solutions in different electrolytes at 60 ◦C, aligns with the battery test observations.
In DME/DOL electrolyte without LiNO3, Li metal reacted aggressively with long-chain poly­ sulfides at elevated temperature.
The HPLC chromatogram (Fig. 2 (C)) shows only short-chain polysulfide (S3 2−) and medium-chain polysulfides (S4 2−and S5 2−) in very low abundance.
In a cycling Li-S battery, those D.

soluble short- and medium-chain polysulfides can return to the cathode, causing severe shuttle effect, as shown in Fig. 1 (C).

Although Li metal in sulfolane electrolyte without LiNO3 also reacts significantly with long-chain polysulfides at elevated temperature as shown in Fig. 2 (G), it exhibits better stability against long-chain poly­ sulfides compared to Li in DME/DOL electrolyte without LiNO3, as seen at room temperature in Fig. 2(F).

Consequently, the polysulfide shuttle effect in a Li-S battery with sulfolane electrolyte without LiNO3 was less severe than in a Li-S battery with DME/DOL electrolyte without LiNO3 even at elevated temperature.

Given that the shuttle-inhibition mechanism in Li-S batteries using DME/DOL electrolyte is associated with reductive decomposition of LiNO3 additive, which plays a role in forming the SEI on the Li anode during cycling [43], it’s reasonable to relate the SEI layer on the Li anode in the sulfolane electrolyte to this mechanism, as indicated by previous XPS analysis [20,33,44].

metal with sulfolane electrolytes were inconclusive and don’t rule out other factors which could also contribute to the shuttle inhibition.
For example, in the early work by S.
[23], a series of electrolytes with a binary solvent composition of sulfolane and DME were tested.
The results clearly showed that when the sulfolane to DME volume ratio decreased to 7:3, the polysulfide shuttle effect emerged and negatively impacted the performance of Li-S battery.
Fundamentally, the poly­ sulfide shuttle phenomenon originates from the thermodynamically favorable reaction between lithium metal and long-chain polysulfides.
This makes the shuttle phenomenon inevitable, and can only be miti­ gated through kinetic approaches as demonstrated in numerous studies on Li-S batteries with nonaqueous liquid electrolytes [4–7].
As a result, most strategies to mitigate polysulfide shuttle effect in Li- S batteries focus on slowing down or restricting the reaction between long-chain polysulfides and Li anode kinetically.
Therefore, any physical or chemical properties of electrolytes that influence the reaction could affect the polysulfide shuttle effect.
For instance, the viscosity of sulfo­ lane electrolytes is much higher than that of DME/DOL electrolytes as shown in Table 1.

This high viscosity could be a reason for the different cycling performance observed: the sulfolane electrolyte might kineti­ cally slow down mass transfer due to its high viscosity thereby miti­ gating the polysulfide shuttle effect even without LiNO3 additive.
In contrast, the low viscosity of DME/DOL electrolyte could accelerate the mass transfer, promoting the polysulfide shuttle effect in the absence of LiNO3 additive.
Fig. 1(E) and (F) display the cycling performances of Li-S batteries in sulfolane electrolyte and DME/DOL electrolyte, both with 0.5 M LiNO3 additive at 60 ◦C.
With the help of the LiNO3 additive, Li-S batteries cycling at elevated temperature show a minimized polysulfide shuttle effect in both electrolytes.

For sulfolane electrolyte with LiNO3, at elevated temperature, the viscosity is lower than that of sulfolane electrolyte without LiNO3.
However, the shuttle effect for Li-S battery with sulfolane electrolyte without LiNO3 was more pronounced than in those using sulfolane electrolyte with LiNO3.
It is likely due to the different SEI compositions on Li metal surfaces for sulfolane electrolyte with and without LiNO3 as demonstrated by the study of SEI composition in DME/DOL electrolytes. 4.
Conclusion Sulfolane electrolytes show promising nonaqueous electrolytes for various lithium-based rechargeable batteries.
Our preliminary study indicates that sulfolane electrolyte can significantly reduce the poly­ sulfide shuttle effect in Li-S batteries at room temperature even without LiNO3 additive.
One possible reason for this inhibition effect is the very high viscosity of sulfolane electrolyte, which could kinetically slow down the diffusion of polysulfides between cathode and lithium anode.
Additionally, the difference in the SEI composition on lithium anode surface could also contribute to this effect.

However, at elevated tem­ perature, which thermodynamically and kinetically favors the poly­ sulfide shuttle, a severe polysulfide shuttle effect was observed in the Li- S batteries with sulfolane electrolyte without LiNO3.
Only when LiNO3 is added to the sulfolane electrolyte can the polysulfide shuttle effect be effectively mitigated at higher temperature in a Li-S battery.
Therefore, while sulfolane electrolyte shows some advantages, it is ultimately a compromised solution, similar to DME/DOL electrolyte, for the use Li-S batteries.
